body: Outside, the arrivals curb is the busiest night of the year with its engine running: exhaust hanging blue under the concrete overhang, a cop in a reflective vest waving cars along with his whole arm, a family hugging in a knot around a car seat. Jack has Gloria’s pie in its white box against his chest and two holy cards in his shirt pocket behind the phone. Theo stands beside him with a leather weekender that has somebody else’s initials stamped by the handle, in the camel coat, which in this wind is a decorative choice.

The Silverado comes up the lane announcing itself with the muffler, his father’s left arm out the window where the blinker ought to be. And it’s clean. Washed, in November — the forest green gone deep, the rust over the rear wheel wells shining like it’s been told it’s going somewhere. “Costigan,” Theo says, pulling his sunglasses down out of his hair to get a better look at it, at night, “that truck has been *detailed*.”
Frank gets out and comes around the hood with the engine running. He has the Browns knit hat on, and under it, at his ears, the gray has come in since August.

s02.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:50 PM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE FRONT DOOR
body: The porch light is on, and the glass in the storm door throws it back at the street. It’s a narrow two-story frame house a few blocks from Brownlee Woods, the same as the houses on either side except for the yard: the glider on the front porch under its winter tarp, which has come half off, and in the side yard Nonna’s bathtub Madonna, white in the streetlight, with her hands out.
Frank cuts the engine, and before anybody has touched a bag he says to Theo, “Come see the garage.” Theo goes, in both coats.

That’s Gina’s window. She’s out the storm door while Jack is still getting the pie out of the cab — Ursuline sweatpants, a Diet Coke, the glow of the basement Dell somehow still on her face — and she takes his sleeve and pulls him into the vestibule and shuts the inside door on the kitchen noise. Then, at a whisper that could strip paint:
“SHE’S. ON. TV.”
“I know, G. You told me. In Denver.”

“I told you on the *phone*. This is *in person*.” She has his sleeve in both fists. Behind the inside door’s glass somebody is running water and a pot lid is rattling. “Do you know what I’ve been doing since Denver? I’ve been *breathing wrong*. Since *Denver*, Jack.”

body.text: “Your Facebook detective,” she whispers, “reporting.”

body: She has done eight hours. She has the show’s website, an episode guide, the fan page — “*Fans*, Jack. Four thousand and something. It doesn’t say *friends*. It went up eleven since *dinner*. I’ve been *refreshing*” — and Kelsey thinks she’s doing a *project*. She’s been in Nonna’s chair at the front window since *seven*; the rosary’s on the sill to make room for her. And Danny called. At eight, with Ma still up at St. Elizabeth’s and Pop at the airport, and Gina took it on the kitchen phone and held. “He said I sounded weird. I said I have mono. I said *nothing*, Jack. I said nothing so hard I gave myself a headache.” He wanted to know if Jack had landed. Gina said she didn’t know. She knew. She had been following the plane on the internet since it left Denver, a little airplane on a map, forty minutes late. He said to tell Jack: *Bring the rich one Friday. Tell him don’t wear nothing nice.*
“You did good, G.”
“I *know* I did good. I’m *dying*. Ma doesn’t know. Pop doesn’t know. Nonna’s in the *hospital*. And the rich one is in the *garage*, Jack. He’s *right there*.”
Jack, who has been holding a pie since Santa Barbara, sets it down on the radiator cover between the boots. “G. Breathe.”
“I *can’t*. I have *mono*.”

She reaches into the waistband of her sweatpants and comes out with a sheet of paper folded in quarters, and holds it out low, by one corner. It’s the dock picture. She printed it on Ma’s printer, in Ma’s color ink, which in this house is saved for report cards and Mass cards.

body: The kitchen at nine at night smells like tomorrow: onion and celery going soft in a pound of butter, a stockpot of turkey necks on the back burner, sweet potatoes in foil, Folgers. Every burner is going. His mother is home from St. Elizabeth’s twenty minutes and still in her coat.

She hugs Jack first, hard, buttons and all. Then she holds Theo out at arm’s length in Frank’s parka and keeps him there, reading him. “Sit,” she says. He sits. Inside a minute there’s a bowl of wedding soup in front of him, and bread, and the good butter. “It’s not dinner,” Maria tells him. “It’s a snack.”

body.text: Theo, aside, over the spoon: “You weren’t exaggerating.”

body: To Jack, with her cold hand on his face: “Did you eat? Don’t lie to me.” He says he ate on the plane. There’s a bowl in front of him anyway.

Theo has a hostess gift in the weekender: a wooden box with a brass clasp, and inside, on a velvet bed, like a watch, a small bottle of something dark. “What is it?” Frank says. “Vinegar, sir.” “In a *box*?” Maria puts it on the shelf with the good dishes. When Theo slides the box across the oilcloth Jack sees the back of his hand, where a line of Italian in blue ballpoint has been written over the ghost of *Glenwood*.

Rosie is asleep upstairs. She left a crayon drawing on the refrigerator, under the St. Brigid’s magnet, that Maria says she made “from what your father told her”: a prince, with yellow hair, a crown and a red car. Theo looks at it over his first bowl, and again over his second, and once more on his way past to the sink.

Through the doorway the front room is dark but for the streetlight, and Nonna’s chair by the window has its rosary back over the arm. “Tomorrow morning,” his mother says, “God willing. And she’ll be furious about the food.”

Under Jack’s blanket the RAZR lights the ceiling. It’s twenty to eleven where she is.

s04.slug: THURSDAY · 9:15 AM · ST. ELIZABETH HEALTH CENTER, 6 WEST
body: Thanksgiving morning, 6 West is running on half a staff and a sense of occasion, and the window at the end of the hall is full of a sky the color of a nickel, down over the parking deck and the wet roofs of the North Side. The nurse at the station has on a turkey-print scrub top and has taped a paper pilgrim hat to her monitor, and his mother is at the counter signing the discharge papers one page at a time, reading every word, because she is a school secretary and knows what people slip into page four. His father is downstairs with the truck running. Gina and Rosie are down in the lobby because of the flu rules, so Jack and Theo go up alone.

Nonna is in the chair beside the bed, dressed since six. Carmela Rinaldi, eighty-four, in her navy housedress with her good cardigan over it: a cast from her knuckles to her elbow, six black stitches over one eyebrow, a heart monitor clipped to the housedress like a pager with its wire running down inside. Somebody has pinned up her hair. The San Giovanni rosary is wound around the good wrist, and her pocketbook is on her knees, held by the good hand, ready. On the tray table sits Gloria’s pecan pie, a quarter gone. His mother brought it up at seven. Nonna had it for breakfast.

Jack kisses her and tells her about the pie: a woman named Gloria, on her feet thirty years, who said Nonna would know what that means. Nonna looks at the pie, and at the quarter of it that isn’t there anymore. “Brava,” she says.

He takes the two holy cards out of his shirt pocket. She holds up Lena’s first — Our Lady of Prompt Succor, gold behind the crown — and turns it over, and finds her own name on the back, in red. *Carmela Rinaldi.* “Questa è della suora?”
“Yes, Nonna.”
St. Raphael next, with his staff and his fish. “E questa?”
“Becca’s.”
“L’altra,” Nonna says. One goes into her missal and one into her pocketbook, and she snaps the pocketbook shut.
Now she looks past Jack at Theo, who has been waiting by the door in two coats, and her eyebrows go up, the stitched one more slowly. “È questo?”
“È questo, Nonna. Theo.”
She crooks the good hand. He comes. She takes his face in it, the cast held off to one side, and turns it toward the window like produce.
Theo lets her. When she lets go he straightens, puts a hand over his heart, and delivers the line off the back of his hand, beautifully, rolling the *r*:
“*Voglio una donna!*”
Jack’s Italian is church and kitchen, but it covers that. He shuts his eyes.
Nonna smacks the back of Theo’s hand with her good one, hard. Theo shakes the hand out, unbowed. “My namesake,” he tells Jack. “Fellini. He spends the whole picnic up a tree.”

Nonna is not interested in Fellini. She takes the hand she smacked, turns it palm down on her knee, and gives him, word by word, sharp, what a boy says to a signora: “*Piacere, signora. Grazie dell’ospitalità.*”
“Piacere, signora,” Theo says. “Grazie dell’*ospedalità*.”
“Ospi-ta-li-tà.”
Theo inclines his head, receiving it. Nonna lets go of the hand and says to Jack, of Theo, “*Troppo magro.*”
Jack translates exactly that much. “Too thin.”
“I’ve been told,” says Theo.

The nurse puts her head in: a wheelchair to the door, it’s policy. Nonna says no in two languages. Theo bows to her from the waist — a real bow, parka and all — and holds it, and Nonna looks at the bow for a while and says, “Va bene,” and sends him for the chair. His mother leans in the doorway with the papers under her arm just long enough to see a boy from Los Angeles bowing to her mother, and goes back to the desk with her hand over her mouth.
And Jack and Nonna are alone in the room with the pie.

She looks at him with her morning eyes. The mornings are the sharp ones; the afternoons come and go now. She looks at him until he looks back. She puts her good hand on his chest, over the St. Michael under his shirt.
“*Tuo fratello porta la tua croce.*”
And at once, in the same voice: “*Dove sono le mie pantofole?*”

response: “Lo so, Nonna.”
She pats his chest twice, like she’s settling a bill. “Le pantofole.”

Theo comes back with the wheelchair, and Nonna is installed in it like a queen on a float: pocketbook on her knees, the pie on the pocketbook, the cast up on the armrest where people can see it. The elevator. The lobby, and Rosie, in her church coat, who runs at the chair from across it shouting *Nonna* and has to be caught. Gina takes the handles from Theo, mortified to be seen pushing anything anywhere near him, and over the top of Nonna’s head gives Jack a look that says *I am holding a secret and a wheelchair at the same time*.

s05.slug: THURSDAY · 12:40 PM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE KITCHEN
body: Louis Prima is going full tilt about Angelina from the counter player, wedged between the bread box and the Sacred Heart calendar, loud enough to carry over the Lions in the front room and Frank telling the Lions what they’re doing wrong. Every burner is lit. The window over the sink has steamed to the frame, and Glenwood Avenue past it is a gray smear with a mailbox in it.

Nonna can’t use her right hand, so she has requisitioned Theo’s. She sits in a kitchen chair pulled up to the counter in her good housedress, the cast across her lap, the heart monitor clipped at her collar, and runs him in Calabrese and the English she keeps for emergencies: *no*, *more*, *there*. The meatballs are the size she says. She makes a ring of her good thumb and finger, and Theo, who has not taken off the Browns parka since the airport and has pushed its sleeves to the elbows, brings each one to the ring for approval before it goes in the pan. The gravy goes one way, with the clock. When he stirs it the other way she says “*No*,” and the spoon stops in the pot as if it heard her. The cardoons go into the oil one at a time. Three in, Theo asks what they are.
“Thistles,” Jack says from the sink, and Theo lowers the next one in with new respect.

After the meatballs, the pie. The quart jar Maria carried up from the basement last night stands open on the counter, Nonna’s August peaches gone gold and slack in their own syrup, and the dough comes out of the icebox in waxed paper. Theo rolls it under orders. The first round tears down the middle, and Nonna says something short about his mother that Jack decides not to translate. The second comes out the shape of Lake Erie. The third holds. She lets him wind it onto the pin and unroll it over the tin, and he gets it there whole and steps back with his floury hands up like a surgeon. She takes over the edge herself, one-handed, her thumb walking the rim — press and turn, press and turn — sixty years of pies in the joint of it.
Gina is helping. This means she is sitting on the counter by the stove in her Ursuline sweatshirt, eating the black olives off the relish tray one at a time and supervising.
“Do you even know what a pierogi *is*.”
A foil pan of them from the St. Brigid’s Altar and Rosary sale is waiting its turn for the oven. Theo examines it. “Is it a type of pasta?”
Gina shuts her eyes. “Oh my *God*.”

“Counselor,” Theo says, “I grew up in Los Angeles. Everything I know about food came to me on a menu.” He reaches for an olive and she moves the tray, and he accepts this. With flour to the wrists and total seriousness, he asks, “How was *New Moon*? I’m told it’s divisive.”
“I’ve seen it *twice*.” She points an olive at him. “Team Edward.”
“Jacob, I’m afraid.”

The tops of Gina’s ears go red. She eats four olives in a row, fast.
Maria put the apron on Jack herself — ST. BRIGID’S FISH FRY 2006, a fish in a chef’s hat — and the RAZR in its front pocket goes off against his hip while he’s scrubbing the meatball pan.

s06.slug: THURSDAY · 2:30 PM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE DINING ROOM
body: The dining room gets the last of the afternoon through the lace curtains and the overhead fixture both, and everything on the table shines a little more than it would in a better house: the good cloth with the grapes around the border, both leaves in, the gravy boat from the wedding, the lasagna beside the turkey as God and Calabria intended, the cranberry sauce still holding the ridges of the can, the cardoons, which every year are a mistake and every year are gone. The folding chair from the basement is at the far corner for whoever’s youngest, and Rosie is in it in her good dress, already into a roll. In the front room the Lions are on with the sound off.

There’s one empty place that isn’t the folding chair. Theo is still on his feet by the sideboard, waiting to be told. His mother stands behind the empty chair with a plate in her hands and doesn’t set it down.
Nonna points the cast at it. “Siediti lì.”
Frank looks at his plate. Theo sits. Maria puts the plate down in front of him, and her hand rests flat on the cloth beside it, and then she picks up the basket of rolls and passes it.
“Guest says it,” Frank says, from the end by the kitchen door.
It’s the rule at this table, older than Jack: whoever is newest says the grace. Theo looks up. “Mr. Costigan, I don’t —”

Frank waits. Nonna waits, her good hand already folded over the cast. Rosie puts her roll down and folds her hands under her chin like a professional. Theo looks across at Jack, once, and Jack can’t help him.
Theo puts his head down.

“Thank you for asking me,” he says. “Thank you for Mrs. Rinaldi, who, Jack tells me, fell going up the stairs for her good rosary, and came home this morning. Thank you for the food, which I’m told is not dinner. It’s a snack.” He stops. “And for the ones who aren’t at this table.” He seems not to know how a thing like this ends. “Amen?”

His mother is crying. She cries at grace every year; this year she cries at this one, on her feet at the corner by the kitchen with the dish towel over her shoulder, and makes no sound about it at all.
“Amen,” Frank says.
“That was *long*,” says Rosie, and Gina kicks her under the table.

Maria wipes her eyes with the corner of the dish towel and says, “Eat,” and the noise comes back into the room all at once — the serving spoons, the chairs, Frank asking for the dark meat like it’s a union grievance.

The bowls go around. The turkey, the lasagna, the pierogi Theo now knows the name of, the cardoons, three of which he takes out of loyalty. Nonna watches him eat the way she watches the street from her chair, and what she sees is a boy taking small bites and talking instead of chewing, and it offends her.

The RAZR goes off in Jack’s pocket against the chair, a dry buzz in the wood that he feels in his back teeth. No phones at this table. Gina’s lives in her waistband at every meal and has since she was thirteen, under a détente that has never been discussed, and Gina doesn’t look up. Not yet.

Nonna turns her chair to Theo and lays the cast on the cloth beside his plate and says something fast in Calabrese. Jack catches a third of it — *mangia*, and *ossa*, bones, and *mamma*. His Italian is church-and-kitchen, and she knows it to the word. She doesn’t even look at him.
“Regina.”
Gina sits up like she’s been called to the board. “She says,” Gina says, “you’re too skinny, and is your mother dead.”
“*Regina*,” says Maria.
“She *said* it. She said *è morta*. I’m just the *translator*.”
Theo puts his fork down. “My mother,” he tells Nonna, “is alive, and has a life coach.”

Gina turns to Nonna and does her best. Jack hears *una signora* and *la vita* and *allenatore* — a football coach — and then Gina gives up on the Italian and mimes a whistle and a clipboard. Nonna looks at Theo over her stitches for some time. At last she makes a small sound in her nose, and that’s the review.
“I told her it’s like a priest,” Gina reports, “but you pay him.”
Nonna has a follow-up. *E il padre?*
“And your dad,” Gina says. She has the floor now and knows it.
“In Cabo,” says Theo. “For the holiday.”
“*Messico*,” Gina tells her, and Nonna says something brief and final, and Gina turns back to Theo with real pleasure. “She says Mexico isn’t a family.”
Theo inclines his head to Nonna across the corner of the table. “Signora,” he says, “I’ve been saying that for years.”
The RAZR goes again. Gina’s eyes drop to his pocket and go straight up to the light fixture, and her face holds its breath.
Nonna isn’t finished. *È cattolico? Va a missa?*
“Is he Catholic,” Gina says, recovering, “and does he go to Mass. She means *do* you. Not *have* you ever.”
Theo tells the truth. “I was baptized for my grandmother. I sit outside.”
Gina, with relish: “He sits *outside*.”

“*Fuori!*” Nonna puts her good hand to her heart, scandalized clear down to her slippers, and the table laughs — Frank into his napkin, Rosie because everybody else is. Theo, under fire, tries his phrase. He turns to her with his hand on his chest. “Piacere, signora. Grazie dell’ospitalietà.”
“*Ospitalità*,” says Nonna, without looking at him, and points the serving spoon at Gina, who puts more lasagna on his plate.

The RAZR goes a third time. While Theo is still turned to Nonna, Gina looks Jack dead in the eye across the cranberry sauce and shapes a word with her mouth that is unmistakably *Cassidy*, and Jack finds her foot under the table and stands on it.
Nonna asks the last one in the same voice, with nothing changed in it at all: “E tua madre — prega per te?”
Gina opens her mouth to be funny and shuts it again. “She wants to know,” she says, “does your mom pray for you.”
Theo looks at his plate. “I don’t think anybody does, Mrs. Rinaldi.”
Gina hasn’t started on it. Nonna, who has enough English for *anybody* and not much else, answers him herself.
“Da stasera, io.”
Gina says it so quietly that Jack, across the table, almost misses it. “She says starting tonight, she does.”
Theo picks up his fork.
“Mangia,” says Nonna, sharp as a rap on the knuckles, and points at his plate with the cast.

And the RAZR goes off a fourth time, right on top of her, loud against the chair in the quiet. His mother, on her feet at the far side of the table with the gravy boat, reaches across the cranberry sauce and holds out her hand to him, palm up, without a word — the way she has held it out for twenty-two years of contraband: squirt guns, notes passed at Mass, a Game Boy at Midnight Mass.

body: The pie comes out at twenty past three on the cake stand Maria keeps for Easter, and so, in a manner of speaking, does the phone. It’s in her apron pocket, and every so often her apron buzzes.

The first time, she’s cutting. The knife stops in the crust. Her eyebrows go up, and she finishes the slice and slides it onto Nonna’s plate with her eyebrows still up, and lets them come back down on their own time. Her hand stays on the knife. Jack once watched her carry a letter addressed to Gina around the house for two days rather than open it. Whatever is buzzing at her hip is not hers to read.

It’s a good pie. Nonna’s August peaches; Theo’s crust, thick on the side where Lake Erie used to be; Nonna’s thumbprints around the rim. Frank eats a piece, says, “Pie’s good,” and holds out his plate for another. Theo receives this with a small bow from the waist, sitting down.

Rosie has fallen asleep against Frank’s arm with a fork in her fist. Nonna slides the last piece onto Theo’s plate with her good hand, and when he opens his mouth about it she points at it with the cast, and he eats it.

body: By ten after five the window over the sink has gone from gray to black, and Jack can see himself in it, and his mother beside him with the towel. He washes and she dries. It has been that way since he could reach the taps.

“Eleven,” she says.
He looks at her.

He dries his hands on the fish in the chef’s hat and opens the phone. The newest is on top.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard. Thanksgiving: told her mom at the table. Texted me first — happy Thanksgiving, praying for Nonna, taking it down now. Then she did.

s08.slug: THURSDAY · 8:15 PM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE FRONT ROOM
body: The front room has gone blue: the TV off, the streetlight on, and the house at the stage of Thanksgiving where everybody is lying on something. Nonna is asleep in her chair by the window with the cast on a sofa pillow and the San Giovanni beads stopped in her good hand somewhere in the third decade. Rosie was carried up at seven. Theo is on the rug with his back against the couch and his hands folded over the parka, over the pie.
Jack dials at a quarter past eight. On Dupre Street it’s a quarter past seven, and she asked.

The other end doesn’t say hello. The phone opens straight onto a room: a television with a crowd in it, men arguing on a back porch over the hiss of a fryer, a woman telling everybody to lower their voices to no effect at all, and over every bit of it a girl screaming that the Saints are ten and oh, TEN AND OH, and the Patriots are going to cry on Monday night, on NATIONAL TELEVISION. Under that, an old woman says something long in French to the room at large.

“You’re on speaker,” Lena says, close to the phone and a little hoarse from shouting over her own family, “with the Broussards and Mémère and a turkey my daddy dropped in four gallons of peanut oil with his eyes shut. Say hi.”
“Hi,” Jack says, and is roared at from New Orleans.
“Put Theo on. I was promised.”
Theo gets up off the rug like he’s been called to the podium. He takes the RAZR in both hands, holds it out at arm’s length, for the cameras, and clears his throat.
“Good evening, New Orleans,” he says. “I’m calling from Youngstown, Ohio, where I have just finished my second piece of peach pie and a tall glass of *pop*.”

The roar comes out of the little speaker so loud it buzzes. Somebody bangs a table. The screaming girl screams “AGAIN,” and Lena, off the phone, says “Josie, he *heard* you,” and Theo does it again, slower, with feeling, a man giving the people what they came for — “a *tall* glass, of *pop*” — and Mémère wants to know in French what on earth, and somebody tells her in French, and she laughs like a gate.

Theo hands the phone back, bows from the waist to the chair where Nonna is sleeping, and goes out through the dining room to the kitchen. The back door bangs. A minute later, across the yard, the garage radio comes up a notch: Frank has the night game.
On Dupre Street a door shuts too, and the Broussards drop to a wall’s worth of noise.
“I’m in my old room,” Lena says. “Sitting on the floor with my back against the door so nobody can come in and ask me where the foil is. Hi, Youngstown.”
“Hi.”
“How’s Theo doing in captivity?”

He tells her about the table. The chair — Danny’s; his father at the end saying the guest says it; Theo with his head down and Rosie with her hands folded under her chin. He gets as far as the food — not dinner, Theo had been told, a snack — and then he’d rather not do the rest of it in his own voice, on the phone, with his grandmother asleep across the room. “He said it,” Jack says.
“Lord,” Lena says, softly, and leaves it there. “And Nonna? Is she home? Did my saint work?”
“She’s home. She’s asleep in her chair about eight feet from me, with a cast up to here. She kept your saint. She put one in her missal and one in her pocketbook, and I didn’t see which went where.”
“Missal,” Lena says at once. “Obviously the missal. I can feel it from here.”

body.text: “Mémère lit two,” she says. “The one at St. Bernard’s Tuesday, and another one this morning before the turkey. She says it was nothing. Carmela Rinaldi.” She says the whole name, first and last, the way it’s written on the back of the card.

“And your daddy?”

“Sober. He drove us.”

“Good.”

He says it’s a tradition. He sounded about nine years old.” She says it fondly, and quick, and is already on to the next thing.

response: “Is that him?”

“In the kitchen with Luc.” She doesn’t pretend she didn’t hear it too. “He brought his mama’s sweet potato pie, and he’s been helping Daddy with the fryer, and he asked Mémère how her hip was, in French, *badly*.” She breathes out through her nose. “Everybody’s being so nice I could scream.”
He lets the laugh go by and starts to tell her about the cardoons.
She tells him anyway, over the top of the cardoons. “Wes is here,” she says. “It’s fine. It’s Thanksgiving.” And then, in her own voice again: “What’s a cardoon?”
“Somebody’s having fun.”
“That’s Wes.” Flat and fast, no trim on it. “Luc brought him. He brought his mama’s sweet potato pie. Don’t you dare be funny about the pie. It’s a very good pie.”

body: She’s telling him about the fryer — her father in safety goggles from the hardware store, Remy standing by with a fire extinguisher he bought for the occasion and has named — when the RAZR goes off against his ear.

It isn’t a ring. It’s the dry hard buzz of a text, straight through the bone behind his ear, the phone shivering with it, and it goes down the line to New Orleans as clear as anything Theo said. He can’t see the screen without taking the phone away from her. In California it’s twenty past five.
“Is that you buzzing?”

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. It’s Nonna’s first morning back, and Nonna is in her chair at the front window in the gray light with the monitor clipped to her collar, telling the San Giovanni beads with her good hand; Gina and Rosie are staying with them.

Theo comes down the stairs dressed for a day of meetings — navy cashmere, gray trousers, his good loafers — and sets four paper rolls of quarters on the counter beside the bag, in a neat row. “Forty dollars,” he says. “I was told quarters.”

His mother looks at the rolls. She picks up two, opens her purse on the chair, puts them in it, snaps it shut, and tips the other two into the bag. Theo opens his mouth. She looks at him. He closes it.
She looks at the rest of him. “No,” she says. “Not the — *no*.”
“It’s my most modest sweater.”
“It’s blue.” She has the sleeve between her finger and thumb already. “Nothing blue. Nothing nice. Nothing they wear.”

Inside, the lobby is cinderblock painted the yellow of old piano keys, and warm, and busy: a sign-in book on a counter, a line of mothers and wives holding their IDs out ready, a wall of lockers with keys on red plastic tags. Over the lockers somebody has painted VISITING HOURS in tall blue capitals, and under it a mural that somebody painted badly and with love — a sun with a face, a rainbow going down into a lake, a family of ducks in a row, a red barn. The officer at the desk reads Jack’s license and looks up. “Costigan. You’re Maria’s.” “Yes, sir.” “How’s your mother holding up?” “Good. My grandmother came home yesterday.” “Tell her I said.”

At the lockers Jack’s hand goes to his shirt pocket out of habit and finds it flat. Coats in, keys in. The quarters ride in their clear bag. Theo goes through the metal detector like he’s done it at better airports, and the officer runs a stamp over the backs of their hands and holds each one under a little purple lamp to see it take: a mark that isn’t there until the light finds it.

Then a steel door, and a box of painted cinderblock the size of an elevator, and another steel door. The first has to close before the second will open, and it takes its time about it. Danny comes through the far door with his hands already out. Twenty-two, in the state blues, his shoulders gone square from push-ups, a haircut somebody inside gave him with more confidence than skill. He has their father’s face from the wedding pictures on the stairs, and the gentlest eyes in the room. journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying.

They look like celery with a grudge, and every stalk has strings down its back that have to come out by hand and little thorns along the leaf edges, and the second a cut end meets the air it starts to go brown, so it goes straight into the big bowl of lemon water at his mother’s elbow. Nonna directs from a kitchen chair by the radiator, the cast in her lap, pointing out the stalks he has ruined. s16b.slug: SUNDAY · 2:20 AM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE FRONT PORCH
body: The porch is the streetlight’s. The moon went down hours ago, and Glenwood Avenue lies there under the one lamp at the curb two doors up in a wash of orange, parked cars and bare maples and wet black asphalt, no snow anywhere. He pulls the tarp the rest of the way off the glider and sits, and the chains take his weight with two cold complaints. Nonna’s afghan goes around his shoulders, brown and orange and gold, and his father’s Browns hat comes down over his ears. His breath goes out in front of him and hangs. Under the boards, through the foundation, the furnace kicks on again and the ducts start up their ticking where he can feel it more than hear it.
Behind him, on the other side of the window glass, Nonna’s chair is empty. In the side yard the bathtub Madonna is a white shape with her hands out.

Before he can say anything she laughs — because she can hear his teeth, it turns out. Her voice isn’t her texts. It isn’t anything like her texts. It’s slower, and lower, and a little hoarse at the bottom, with a whole day of people worn into it, and it comes into his ear from Studio City close enough to feel.
“You’re *outside*.”
“Everybody’s asleep.”
“It’s *Ohio*. In *November*.”
“Yeah.”
“Go inside.”
“No.”
That’s the deal.

What he typed in the basement is somewhere in the phone all along. She doesn’t bring it up. He doesn’t either. It’s in how low she keeps her voice. And he wants her — on his father’s porch at half past two, in his grandmother’s afghan, from the other side of the country — and he keeps his own voice down and lets the wanting be exactly what it is, and goes no closer to it than that.

“All right, here’s Thanksgiving,” she says. “*Thanksgiving at My Mother’s.* A one-woman show. One act, no intermission, please silence your Ohio.” He hears her settle into something soft, a couch, a bed. “Act one. The turkey arrives. In a van. With a handler. Nobody in the house has touched it with their hands.”

She does the handler — a calm young man in black who needs a signature. She does twenty-two people in a living room in Studio City who want something, one at a time, quick changes: a man who manages a boy band and has a horror picture shooting in Romania, very prestigious, she’d play a nun; somebody’s cousin with her phone already up, *it’s for my niece, she’s your biggest fan, can you just say her name, it’s Madison, no, say it like Cassidy*; a woman from her mother’s Pilates class who asks if she’s seeing anyone and then answers for her. She does a dentist with a screenplay, and Jack is laughing too hard by then to be any help to the dentist.

“And one parrot,” she says, “who’s honest. He sat on the curtain rod all afternoon and told the truth about my mother, and everybody pretended he was saying hello.” A rustle. “Fin. Thank you. You’ve been a wonderful house.” Then, in her own voice: “Your turn. Do your family. I’ve been reading about them for three days. I want the voices.”

response: He sets it up for her: the table, somebody saying something impressive, his father not lifting his eyes off his plate. Then he puts the voice on — low, flat, out of the side of the mouth, Glenwood Avenue to the bone. “Close your mouth. You’ll catch flies.”
“Again.”
He does it again.

“Again. Slower. Where’s his fork?” He tells her where the fork is. He does it a third time, with the fork, and she’s quiet, and then she does it back to him, badly, in a voice that is nothing like his father and is somehow, against all odds, the plant — a man on a line, out of patience, kind about it. “*Close your mouth.* Is that close?”
“That’s close.”
“I’m going to use that on everybody.”

So he does Nonna. He pulls the afghan up like a shawl, though there’s nobody to see it, and drops his voice into her chest, and points with a cast he doesn’t have at her plate in Studio City. “*Mangia.*” And then Thanksgiving morning, all of 6 West at her service and a wheelchair at the door, and the only thing she wants to know: where are her slippers.
Skye doesn’t laugh. She’s quiet a while.
“She’s the best one,” she says.
He takes a breath of the November air and gives it to her at full volume, Gina on the basement floor with her hair in her face: “*JACK. SHE’S ON TV.*”

It goes off the front of the porch and down Glenwood Avenue like a car alarm. Two houses down a dog wakes up and has an opinion. In Studio City something hits the floor — the phone — and from a long way off, from the floor, he can hear her laughing, helpless, the kind that won’t let a person up, and it goes on for a while before there’s a scrape and a rustle and her breath close again.
“I dropped you,” she says. “I’m sorry. I had to lie down on the rug. Does she really —”
“Exactly like that.”
“I love her. Don’t tell her. Tell her.”

s16c.slug: SUNDAY · 3:05 AM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE FRONT PORCH
body: A car with one headlight comes down Glenwood at five past three, slows for nothing, and turns at the corner. After it the street is the lamp’s again.
“What time is it there?”
“Three.”
“And you have church.”
“Eight o’clock. It’s Advent.”
“What’s Advent?”

He tells her, low, with his breath going up past the porch light. Four Sundays before Christmas. A wreath with four candles, three violet and one rose — pink, if you’re not a priest — and you light one more each week, so the dark gets a little less dark. The readings are about the end of the world and about staying awake for it. Somebody is coming who said He’d come. The point is to be up when He gets here.
“Wait,” Skye says. “You people have a whole *season* for waiting.”
“Four weeks.”

“For *waiting*.” She sounds delighted and a little offended. “I’ve never waited four weeks for anything in my life. I don’t think I’ve waited four *days*.” He can hear her shift on whatever she’s lying on. “So what are *you* waiting for? You personally. Not the candles.”
He looks at the Madonna in the side yard, white in the streetlight with her hands out, in no hurry.
“To be awake when it counts,” he says. “I’m usually not.”
“I’m going to think about that,” she says.
No bit comes after it. On the line there’s a small sound like a pen cap, and then, a while later, she asks him what the candles smell like.

Beeswax, he tells her, and the match, and on the first Sunday the old ladies’ perfume, because the old ladies come early on the first Sunday to see which family from the school got picked to light it.
“Who got picked?”
“I don’t know yet. That’s the suspense.”
“You’re waiting to find out who lights the candle about waiting.”
“Now you’re getting it.”
At ten to four the RAZR gives three small chirps against his ear like something in a nest, and the battery bar on the outer screen is one bar and blinking.
“What was that?”
“Battery. Hang on. Don’t hang up.” He gets up off the glider with the afghan and goes in through the storm door with the phone at his ear.

“And here,” Skye murmurs at once, very soft, very British, “in the frozen north, the Ohio male leaves the safety of his porch. He knows the territory. He steps over the board that talks. He does not wake the elders.” He steps over the board that talks. In the kitchen he finds his charger where he left it, by the bread box. “Note the stealth. Note the hat.”

Back on the porch, the only outlet is the one beside the storm door that his father runs the Christmas lights from, and the cord just reaches the arm of the glider if he sits at that end. He sits at that end.

By four she is quieter. People are, at four. They have been talking about nothing — the Starlite’s jukebox, whether Ohio has a coast (“Lake Erie.” “A puddle with a navy.”) — and then she stops in the middle of it.
“Can I ask you something.”
It doesn’t come up at the end like a question. He pulls the afghan tighter.
“Yeah.”
“Does it matter? The TV part.”
Down the street the dog has gone back to sleep. He thinks of a clear plastic bag of quarters on a low table, and a row of vending machines along a cinderblock wall, humming.

s16d.slug: SUNDAY · 4:35 AM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE FRONT PORCH
body: Past half past four — half past one in Studio City — she starts to slow down. Her sentences get longer and further apart, and she asks him what the street looks like, right now, from where he is.

So he tells her. There’s one streetlight, two doors up, and it buzzes. The cars are all parked facing the same way, because on Glenwood it matters. The neighbors two doors down have an inflatable turkey that stands up eight feet tall when it’s plugged in, and they unplug it at ten, so right now it’s lying face-down on their lawn with its pilgrim hat in the wet grass like it lost an argument. And there’s a Madonna in his own side yard. His grandfather dug the hole for her before Jack was born and stood an old clawfoot bathtub up on its end in it, half buried, and Nonna painted the inside blue, and the Blessed Mother stands in it in white, with her hands held out a little at her sides, palms forward, like she’s —
Somewhere in the middle of the Madonna the line has changed, and he can tell she’s asleep.
“Goodnight,” he tells it, very low, and shuts the phone at 5:08, and the outer screen tells him it was two hours and forty-eight minutes before it goes dark.

He sits a minute more with the cord still running to his father’s outlet. At ten past five he goes in with the afghan, quietly, over the board that talks, and puts it back over the arm of Nonna’s chair where it was, and lies down on the front-room couch in his coat, because the stairs would wake somebody.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Doesn’t go here. Not yet, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Saw Becca on my profile. Says she’s always wanted to play the other woman. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna.

s17.slug: SUNDAY · 5:40 AM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE FRONT ROOM
body: At twenty to six the front room belongs to the streetlight, one long slant of it through the sheers to the foot of the couch, where Jack is lying in his coat with his eyes open. The afghan is back over the arm of Nonna’s chair, where he put it. The house is still enough that he can hear the kitchen clock.
Above him, the seventh stair complains.

Nonna comes down in the dark a step at a time: the good hand on the rail with the rosary wound through its fingers, the cast held against her housecoat, a small green light blinking at her collar. Jack is up on one elbow by the time she reaches the bottom. She doesn’t look at him. She crosses the front room without turning on a lamp, lowers herself into her chair at the window in stages, draws the afghan over her knees with her good hand, and begins. He can hear the beads click against the cast.
He lies back down. The room keeps its quiet.

Through the window, under the streetlight, Theo is coming up Glenwood Avenue from the Market Street end. He has Frank’s parka zipped to his chin, and something held against his chest that flashes when he passes under the light: cellophane. A bunch of carnations, red and white. He turns in at the side yard and crosses the wet grass to Nonna’s bathtub Madonna, crouches, and lays the flowers at her feet. Then he stands up and keeps standing there in the cold, his hands in the parka’s pockets, his breath going up white past her shoulder.
The beads have stopped. In the chair Nonna is watching him too. She doesn’t turn her head toward the couch, and Jack doesn’t say anything to her.
Eventually Theo comes back across the grass. The side door opens and closes without its usual bang, and the stairs take him up, all fourteen. The seventh doesn’t make a sound under him.
At the window Nonna finds her place on the beads and starts again.

s18.slug: SUNDAY · 7:15 AM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE KITCHEN
body: At a quarter past seven the kitchen light is on, and the window over the sink has only just begun to give the yard back: the garage, the clothesline, and at the edge of it the side yard, where the Madonna stands with something red and white at her feet.

Everybody is in church clothes and eating standing up, except Nonna, in black, the cast in a sling Maria made out of a good scarf, and Theo, whom Maria has sat down by force. Theo is wearing one of Frank’s ties, brown, with a pattern like a motel bedspread, and on it Danny’s tie clip. Jack watched his mother fasten it on him at the foot of the stairs, and smooth the tie down twice, and walk away fast.

His father went to the bakery on Midlothian at seven. He came back in by the side door with a white box tied in red-and-white string, and on his way across the kitchen his eyes went out the side window and came back, and he set the box on the table and poured his coffee and said nothing about the yard. So far the yard hasn’t come up.
The box is open now: cannoli, the shells blistered, the ends dipped in chopped pistachio, powdered sugar over everything, including Rosie.

Theo has his iPhone out beside his coffee. Maria puts a cannoli on a napkin in front of him and holds it there until he takes it, and he sets the phone down to take it, face up, still lit, next to the box. Jack reaches across for the box and reads the screen upside down.

s19.slug: SUNDAY · 8:00 AM · ST. BRIGID OF KILDARE, SOUTH SIDE
s19.music: The St. Brigid’s Choir — “O Come, O Come, Emmanuel”
body: St. Brigid’s has gone violet overnight, Fr. Dom and the ambo both, and by the communion rail the wreath on its brass stand, four candles stuck in pine, three violet and one rose. The eight o’clock choir is six people and an organ older than Frank. During the second verse a family from the school comes up the aisle — Maria’s chin comes up as they pass; she knows the mother — and the father lifts the smallest boy to the taper, and the boy lights the first violet candle on his second try.

The Costigans have their pew, two-thirds of the way back on the left. Nonna has the center-aisle end, as she always has, with the cast propped on the back of the pew in front; then Theo, in Frank’s tie; then Rosie and Maria; then Jack and Gina; Frank has the side-aisle end. There’s no Gloria this morning. Rosie, who loves the Gloria, waits for it with her mouth ready, and it doesn’t come.

“The Lord be with you.” “And also with you.” Fr. Dom Bruno, sixty-some and lame in the left knee, reads the Gospel slowly, to people he has known for thirty years. *Be vigilant at all times and pray that you have the strength…*
As he limps to the center for the homily, Gina leans into Jack’s shoulder. “He’s never preached on anything with *wives* in it,” she whispers.

Fr. Dom keeps it short, the way he keeps everything. Staying up for somebody, he says, is the oldest way there is of loving them, and every mother on this street already knows how to do it; he’s only asking them to do it for God as well.

At the consecration the bells go and the pew goes down onto the kneelers, all but Theo, who stays on the seat. Nonna doesn’t look at him. She reaches over with her good hand and puts it on his shoulder and presses, once, firmly, and Theo kneels, in Frank’s tie, beside her.

body.text: Across the side aisle, in the pew opposite, are the Vrabels: Ashley, her mother, her father in a sport coat that pulls across the shoulders. At the sign of peace Gina steps past Frank into the side aisle and holds out her hand to Ashley Vrabel. Ashley looks at it, and takes it. “Peace be with you,” Gina says, and Ashley says it back, and Gina steps back into the pew with her chin up and her face perfectly blank. Over their daughters’ heads, Frank and Mr. Vrabel nod to each other once. Jack, standing beside Gina’s empty place, watches it happen.

After Communion, kneeling, he looks at the one lit candle in the wreath. Since the confession he has said Becca’s name to God every day — in the dark in 412, over sinks, under the blanket in the back bedroom — and this is the First Sunday of Advent, and the penance is done. He can pray for anybody he likes.

journal.title: Gina

Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn.

s20.slug: SUNDAY · 1:00 PM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE GARAGE
body: The radio on the workbench has the Browns in Cincinnati, and the Browns are losing at a steady, professional pace. The space heater keeps the near half of the garage at seventy degrees and leaves the far half in Ohio. Frank has his chair. Theo has the bucket, upside down, in Frank’s parka. Jack has the third chair, the one with duct tape on the seat, pulled out of the corner. Frank opens the Stroh’s fridge and takes out three cans and hands two of them over, one and then the other, and sits. None of them is driving anywhere today.
Frank’s commentary runs to about three words a quarter. First quarter: “Here we go.” Second: “There it is.”

body.text: At the two-minute warning Theo asks about Lordstown, and Frank tells him. He tells him about the Monday in 1983 when he started, twenty-five and scared of the noise; about the line, and how you learn to hear when something’s wrong with it; about June, and the bankruptcy, and the recall list he reads at the union hall every Tuesday; about the small car that might come next year, maybe, if anybody in Detroit can count. Jack has heard most of it before. He has never heard the part about being scared of the noise.
body.else: Theo was promised on Thursday night that if he came out here Sunday he’d see something, and he does: a Browns team committed to losing from the opening kickoff, without flash, like a craftsman. Theo is enchanted. He keeps asking Frank to explain things, and Frank keeps explaining them.

body: At halftime Frank turns off the radio, and the CD player on the shelf over the vise picks up in the middle of Sinatra where it left off, and it’s “That’s Life,” and Frank sings along under it, a word behind, the way he does.
In the third quarter Frank says, “Your old man call?”

“Thursday,” Theo says. “From a boat, in Cabo. Four minutes.” He turns his can around in his hands. “You could hear the boat being expensive.” And then, shorter: “He asked if I needed anything. I said no. He said good.”
Frank lets the Browns punt.
“Your old man’s an idiot,” he says.
Theo looks over at him.
Frank keeps his eyes on the radio. “You come back. Christmas. Whenever. You don’t call first.”
“Thank you, sir.”

On the workbench beside the radio Theo’s iPhone lights up and begins to buzz its way across the plywood toward a coffee can of drywall screws. LANEY, the screen says. Theo looks at it, and lets it ring, and the Bengals score over it.
Fourth quarter, at the gun: “They’re going to be one and eleven.”

His father and his roommate spend the rest of the afternoon arguing about whether the Browns should fire somebody, and if so whom, and how high up. Jack sits in the third chair with his beer going warm in his hand and listens. His father has his boots up on the bucket Theo abandoned and a can on his knee, and he is telling a boy from Los Angeles that he doesn’t know the first thing about football, and he’s laughing while he says it. Jack hasn’t seen him laugh like that since before June. For an afternoon, in a garage, with the Browns at one and ten, his father is happy.

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt. Saturday he called about Ohio State. Overtime. Pasadena. First time since September. Thanksgiving: sober. Washed the truck. Picked us up at Pittsburgh and talked to Theo the whole way home. Guest says grace — his rule. Waited in the truck at Trumbull. Told Theo to come back. You don’t call first.

s21.slug: SUNDAY · 3:40 PM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, NONNA’S CHAIR BY THE FRONT WINDOW
body: By twenty to four the packing is done, and on the dining-room table his mother is assembling Theo’s leftovers like a dowry, a Tupperware at a time, labeling the lids in school-secretary capitals. In the front room the lamp isn’t on yet. Nonna is in her chair at the window with her rosary and her monitor and the afghan, and Jack is on the footstool beside her, which he outgrew around the sixth grade. Out in the side yard, at the Madonna’s feet, the carnations have gone dark in the gray afternoon, and the cellophane has fogged.
The RAZR buzzes on his knee.

body: Twenty to one in Studio City, and she has only just woken up. He smiles at the screen before he can stop.
Nonna isn’t looking at the phone. She’s looking at his face.
“Chi ti scrive?”
He has his mouth open to answer when she answers it herself, sharp, about the one thing she’s sure of. “Non è la suora.”

journal.title: Nonna
journal.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. That was the nineteenth of September. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her the girl has a boyfriend. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’ Purdue Saturday. Dad said ‘Purdue’ and that was the call. Nonna got on the extension and called me Danny. Then she knew me. Then she asked about the crab girl. Sunday the 8th: ‘E la ragazza?’ Which one, I didn’t ask. She didn’t say. Monday she fell on the stairs she’d been keeping off. St. Elizabeth’s: her wrist, six stitches, a monitor for her heart. Called the paramedic handsome. Dad drove her. Home Thanksgiving morning. Cast to the elbow; a monitor on her housedress. Kept both cards — the nun’s and the other one. Made Theo her hands. Sat him in the chair. Says she’ll pray for him, starting that night. Knows it isn’t the nun.

response: “Una ragazza. Fa l’attrice, Nonna.”
“Un’attrice.” She says it darkly, and moves a bead along. “Attento, Giacomino.”
She looks out at the yard. When she turns back, her face is new, and pleased to find him there. “E la ragazza?”
“L’attrice, Nonna. Te l’ho detto.”
“L’attrice,” she says, as though it’s news, and pats his face with her good hand.

s22.slug: SUNDAY · 4:30 PM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE FRONT PORCH → THE SILVERADO
body: The goodbyes on Glenwood Avenue happen on the porch steps in under ten minutes, because that’s how long Frank says the truck will idle before it gets ideas. The light is going. Two houses down somebody has already put the Christmas lights up and is testing them, on and off, on and off.

His mother hands Theo a Giant Eagle bag with four Tupperwares in it, the lids labeled TURKEY. LASAGNA. COOKIES — SHARE. COOKIES — DON’T. It would feed a floor. She hugs him and tells him to call when he lands. He says yes, Mrs. Costigan. She says *call*.

Rosie comes out the storm door at a run with two pieces of paper. One is the prince off the refrigerator, with the magnet marks still in its corners. The other one is new: the same prince, the yellow hair, the crown, the red car, and now a coat down to his knees in orange and brown. She holds them both up at him and doesn’t say anything. Theo takes them and looks at them. He kneels on the porch step, unzips the gray camera bag, lays them in flat on top of the camera, and zips it shut.
Gina is on the top step with her arms crossed in her Ursuline hoodie. “Bye, LA.”
“Counselor.”
When Jack comes up past her for his duffel she says, low enough that it’s only his: “Nobody. I know.”

Nonna is in the storm door in her housecoat with the cast, holding the door open with her hip. She crooks her good hand at Theo. He comes back up the steps, and she presses something into his palm and folds his fingers over it with hers: a twenty, folded small.
Theo looks down at it.
“Per il viaggio,” Nonna says. She keeps her hand closed over his and says something more, low and quick, in the Calabrese that’s only hers. Jack, two steps down, catches *Natale*.
Theo doesn’t reach for the Fellini, or for the phrase off the back of his hand. “Grazie, Nonna,” he says, and it comes out right.
She nods once, for the accent. Jack’s turn is next: the same fold, the same hand closing his fingers over it, the same twenty.

Frank drives them to Pittsburgh. Theo rides in the middle with the camera bag on his knees, and in the side mirror, as the Silverado pulls away from the curb, the carnations sit red at the Madonna’s feet until the corner takes them.

journal.title: Rosie
journal.text: Rosie Costigan, eight. Drew Theo as a prince before she ever met him. Drew him again in Dad’s parka. He kept both.

s23.slug: SUNDAY · 7:50 PM · A REGIONAL JET, WESTBOUND OUT OF PITTSBURGH
body: The window seat is Jack’s again without anybody saying so. Maria’s Giant Eagle bag is under the seat in front of Theo, and the cabin is full of people in Steelers jackets going back to wherever the holiday borrowed them from.
Before the door closes, the RAZR goes off in his hand.

body: He types something back, slowly, one thumb, and sends it, and turns the phone off as the flight attendant comes down the aisle checking belts.

Theo is awake. He has the twenty out of his pocket and is turning it over in his fingers, over and over, through the climb out over the dark of western Pennsylvania, the little towns underneath strung along their rivers in orange.
“Your grandmother told me to come back at Christmas,” he says, without turning his head. His eyes stay on the twenty. “In Calabrese. I think it was that.”
“It was that.”
Theo folds the twenty once more along its creases. He doesn’t put it in his wallet. He puts it in his shirt pocket and buttons the pocket, and the cabin lights go down.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty.

journal.title: Thanksgiving
journal.text: Wes will be at the Broussards’ table on Thanksgiving, like every year since the storm. He carried the twins out of a second floor. Lena says she’d go anywhere nobody knows his name. I’m going to ask her to Youngstown — properly, in a week. Not one breath after Becca’s name. A week to the night, I asked about the table. She’ll be okay. Julian says call him from the bathroom. I didn’t ask the other thing. Becca’s done. It’s me and the Greyhound. Theo’s coming. I asked him at halftime of Michigan; he said yes before I finished. Two seats to Pittsburgh, Wednesday. The Greyhound’s a voucher. Monday Nonna fell. Ma knows about Becca now. Theo and I fly Wednesday — my first time up. Glenwood. Theo in Danny’s bed. Nonna home Thursday. Theo said grace. Trumbull Friday — Theo met Danny. Advent Sunday. Back Sunday night.
